newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan at a loss over how to calm islands dispute.
newsitem.headline: Japan at a loss over how to calm islands dispute.

text.p: Japan says it is at a loss as to how to defuse a growing diplomatic crisis over disputed islands in the East China Sea.
"Do you have any suggestions? We're racking our brains," chief government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told reporters on Thursday.

Pressure on Tokyo to calm anti-Japanese sentiment in regions claiming sovereignty over the islands -- known as the Senkakus in Japan and Diaoyus in Chinese -- escalated after the death of Hong Kong activist leader David Chan on Thursday, when he dived off a ship in a protest against Japanese control.

His death was the first in almost two months of protests in Hong Kong, China, Taiwan and Macau since Japanese right-wing extremists erected a lighthouse on the islands as a symbol of Japanese sovereignty.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Thursday that he was not optimistic that there would be no diplomatic impact from Chan's death.
Nozomu Akizuki, a professor at Tokai University near Tokyo, said Japan is in a dilemma because if it concedes to demands to remove the lighthouse it would also contradict its previous claims.

Akizuki also said it is difficult to calm what he called an "ethnic outrage" with foreign diplomacy. "There is no real solution. A rash action would merely add fuel to the flames. The best thing to do is to remain silent," Akizuki said.

On Friday, Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda refused on Friday to say whether he had promised Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen in a meeting in New York at the weekend that Japan would take action against the right-wingers.

But he said he told Qian that Japan would "carefully deal with the acts of the private group based on the common understanding that this issue must not jeopardise overall relations between the two countries".
Qian asked Ikeda in New York that Japan take "concrete action", but Ikeda urged China in turn to approach the situation reasonably and not let it interfere with relations between the two countries.
Senior Japanese Foreign Ministry officials said the government was not involved in activities of a private group and could only urge involved parties to "approach the matter calmly".
"The government is in no way involved in actions of the rightist group nor do we support their activities," Foreign Ministry spokesman Ken Shimanouchi told a news conference.
"The structure is on private property and it is our understanding that the owner hasn't expressed objection," he said. "Japan has the rule of law... There is a limit to what Japan can do."
Tokyo's claim to the islands dates to 1895, when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories. China has claimed sovereignty over the islands for centuries.

The Taiwan government also claims ownership of the islands. The Hong Kong activists had vowed to reclaim the islands, saying they would remove the lighthouse and raise the red flag of the People's Republic of China.
